item.title: US recession fears rise as falling household wealth and market turmoil point to 25% risk: Report
item.description: Growing concerns over a possible recession in the US are emerging as falling household wealth, weakening housing activity and a sharp stock market correction put pressure on the economy.
item.content:encoded:
US recession fears rise as falling household wealth and market turmoil point to 25% risk: Report Growing concerns over a possible recession in the US are emerging as falling household wealth, weakening housing activity and a sharp stock market correction put pressure on the economy. ANI | Updated: 24-11-2026 11:45 IST | Created: 24-11-2026 11:45 IST

Representative Image (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Growing concerns over a possible recession in the US are emerging as falling household wealth, weakening housing activity and a sharp stock market correction put pressure on the economy. However, the probability of a recession remains at 25 per cent, while the possibility of a market panic followed by a recovery is estimated at 75 per cent, according to an assessment by Ionic Wealth. The report said the US economy is facing pressure as three important sources of household spending power — wages, stock market wealth and home equity — are declining together in real terms during the current quarter. This could affect consumer spending, which has so far helped the economy absorb repeated economic shocks. It stated, “Recession at 25% and a Panic That Reverses at 75%...Most of the concerns behind the selloff point to an AI build out that takes longer, rather than one that stops. A recession needs the Fed and the consumer to fail together”. The report mentioned that the housing market is also showing signs of weakness, with pending home sales falling 17 per cent year-on-year in October. At the same time, households hold a near-record share of their financial assets in equities, making them more vulnerable to falling stock prices. The report highlighted that overall the Nasdaq 100 has fallen 19.8 per cent from its October 5 high, while the S&P 500 has declined 11.6 per cent from its October 6 record. Another concern is the possibility that interest rates may remain high for longer. The report noted that inflation was running at 3.7 per cent and estimated that the Federal Reserve would need to raise interest rates to 6.75 per cent by the end of 2027 to bring inflation down to its 2 per cent target. It said such a rate path would be difficult for both consumers and the US Treasury to sustain. However, the report said the market correction does not necessarily indicate that demand for artificial intelligence (AI) has weakened. It noted that AI infrastructure orders extend into 2028 and 2029, with much of the memory capacity already booked. Under its main scenario, which carries a 75 per cent probability, the current market panic eventually reverses as demand holds and the Federal Reserve eases its stance after December. The alternative scenario, carrying a 25 per cent probability, involves a recession if the Fed continues raising rates through 2027 while household finances remain under pressure. The report said the key factor to watch is whether the Federal Reserve changes its policy direction before further market weakness causes greater damage to household wealth and consumption. The next Federal Reserve (FOMC) policy decision is scheduled for Wednesday, December 9, following the December 8–9 meeting. item.title: UN Human Rights expert urges Pakistan to end "inhumane detention" conditions for former PM Imran Khan
item.description: According to a statement from the OHCHR, Alice Jill Edwards, the UN Special Rapporteur on torture, urged Pakistan to ensure that the 72-year-old former leader's detention aligns with international ...
item.content:encoded:
UN Human Rights expert urges Pakistan to end "inhumane detention" conditions for former PM Imran Khan According to a statement from the OHCHR, Alice Jill Edwards, the UN Special Rapporteur on torture, urged Pakistan to ensure that the 72-year-old former leader's detention aligns with international legal standards, the OHCHR statement noted. ANI | Updated: 24-11-2026 11:20 IST | Created: 24-11-2026 11:20 IST

Former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan (File Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

A United Nations human rights expert has called on Pakistan to take urgent action to address reports of inhumane and undignified prison conditions for former Prime Minister Imran Khan, warning that his treatment could amount to torture or other cruel and degrading practices. According to a statement from the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR), Alice Jill Edwards, the UN Special Rapporteur on torture, urged Islamabad to ensure that the 72-year-old former leader's detention aligns with international legal standards, the OHCHR statement noted. “I call on Pakistani authorities to ensure that Khan’s conditions of detention fully comply with international norms and standards,” Edwards said, according to the OHCHR. Highlighting his treatment since being moved to Adiala Jail in Rawalpindi on September 26, 2023, Edwards pointed to reports that Khan has been kept in prolonged solitary confinement, locked in his cell for 23 hours a day with severely limited contact with the outside world. “Since his transfer to Adiala Jail in Rawalpindi on 26 September 2023, Imran Khan has reportedly been held for excessive periods in solitary confinement, confined for 23 hours a day in his cell, and with highly restricted access to the outside world,” she said, per the OHCHR. “His cell is reportedly under constant camera surveillance.” The Special Rapporteur emphasised that international human rights law prohibits prolonged or indefinite solitary confinement, noting that isolation lasting beyond 15 days constitutes psychological torture, according to the OHCHR. “Khan’s solitary confinement should be lifted without delay. Not only is it an unlawful measure, but extended isolation can also bring about very harmful consequences for his physical and mental health,” Edwards stated. According to information received by the UN expert, Khan is barred from outdoor exercise, prohibited from interacting with fellow prisoners, and prevented from attending communal prayers, the OHCHR reported. In addition, court-authorised meetings with his relatives, legal team, and other visitors are routinely cut short or disrupted. The OHCHR statement also detailed severe physical conditions inside Khan's small cell, which reportedly lacks proper ventilation and natural light. Extreme seasonal temperatures and poor airflow have allegedly resulted in foul odours and insect infestations, leading to reports that Khan has experienced nausea, vomiting, and significant weight loss. “Anyone deprived of liberty must be treated with humanity and dignity,” Edwards said, according to the OHCHR. “Detention conditions must reflect the individual’s age and health situation, including appropriate sleeping arrangements, climatic protection, adequate space, lighting, heating, and ventilation.” Noting that Khan suffers from major underlying medical conditions—including a severe spinal injury sustained in a 2013 accident and gunshot wounds from a 2022 assassination attempt—Edwards raised alarm over his access to healthcare. “Khan has reportedly been denied adequate medical attention,” she said, per the OHCHR. “I urge the authorities to allow a visit by his personal physicians.” The OHCHR added that the Special Rapporteur has formally raised concerns regarding Khan's treatment with the Pakistani government and will continue to monitor the situation. Earlier on Friday, UN Human Rights Chief Volker Türk also called for the immediate release of former Pakistan's Prime Minister Imran Khan as concerns over his deteriorating health mount. In an interview to Christiane Amanpour on CNN, Turk said, “I call for Imran Khan’s release. I call for his proper treatment, and I actually call for de-escalation. We need to diffuse the political tensions that are around this case, which means that a confidence-building measure between the opposition and the government could be his immediate release.” On November 16, Imran Khan issued an urgent open letter from Adiala Jail to the country’s top judges, pleading for immediate medical treatment and the enforcement of unimplemented court orders. He said that he faces a potentially fatal medical emergency and that his wife risks permanent blindness behind bars. The former premier accused jail authorities of holding him in "torturous solitary confinement for up to twenty-two hours a day" since December 20, 2025, the day a verdict was announced in the Toshakhana (Bvlgari) case, cutting him off from family visits, phone calls with his sons, reading materials, and legal counsel. (ANI)

item.title: Sheikh Hasina plans Bangladesh return on December 16, seeks government-arranged flight: Report
item.description: Former Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina plans to return to Bangladesh on December 16, after spending more than two years in exile in India, according to a Reuters report on Tuesday.
item.content:encoded:
Sheikh Hasina plans Bangladesh return on December 16, seeks government-arranged flight: Report Former Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina plans to return to Bangladesh on December 16, after spending more than two years in exile in India, according to a Reuters report on Tuesday. ANI | Updated: 24-11-2026 10:16 IST | Created: 24-11-2026 10:16 IST

Former Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina (File Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Former Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina plans to return to Bangladesh on December 16, after spending more than two years in exile in India, according to a Reuters report on Tuesday. Hasina has urged the government in Dhaka to arrange her air transport from Delhi aboard the national carrier, Biman Bangladesh Airlines, and facilitate the necessary travel documentation. In a statement, her spokesperson Syed Mozammel Ali told Reuters that Hasina wanted the Bangladesh government to facilitate her return on the anniversary of the country's victory in the 1971 Liberation War against Pakistan. "Since Sheikh Hasina was flown to India on a Bangladesh aircraft on August 5th, 2024, she now calls upon the government to arrange for her air transport from Delhi back to Dhaka," Ali told Reuters. "Having exiled her contrary to the Constitution under such circumstances, it is now the responsibility of the government to make possible her return to Bangladesh on Victory Day on December 16th," he added. December 16 is observed as Victory Day in Bangladesh, marking the surrender of Pakistani forces in 1971 and the country's emergence as an independent nation. Meanwhile, Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Monday held talks with leaders of the student-led National Citizen Party (NCP), which emerged from the July-August 2024 protests that led to Hasina's ouster. The meeting, held at the Cabinet Division Secretariat in Dhaka, was part of a series of engagements with political groups involved in the anti-Hasina movement, amid reports of crude bomb explosions, arson and violence in different parts of the country. A four-member NCP delegation led by party Convener Nahid Islam met Rahman. NCP Member Secretary Akhtar Hossain, Senior Joint Convener Hasnat Abdullah and Joint Convener Akram Hossain were also present. According to Bangladesh's state news agency BSS, Prime Minister's Additional Press Secretary Atikur Rahman Rumon said the meeting lasted approximately 40 minutes. Following the interaction, Prime Minister's Office Spokesperson Mahdi Amin described the meeting as reflecting unity among democratic and anti-authoritarian political forces amid attempts to destabilise the country. "Against the fallen autocratic and fascist forces, all democratic and anti-authoritarian political forces are united, regardless of their political views, beliefs and ideologies," Amin told reporters at the Secretariat. He said the engagement demonstrated that political groups could set aside party affiliations and ideological differences when faced with challenges to Bangladesh's political stability. Speaking after the meeting, NCP Convener Nahid Islam emphasised that political dialogue should lead to concrete action rather than remain limited to discussions. "We do not want discussions merely for the sake of discussions. We want dialogue to continue, but we also want to see what steps the government takes to make it fruitful," Nahid said. The NCP emerged from the student-led movement that spearheaded the July-August 2024 protests against Hasina's government, which culminated in her departure from Bangladesh on August 5, 2024. (ANI)

item.title: Oxfam demands independent assessment of "potential contamination" risks in Gaza strip after Israel's military action
item.description: Describing Gaza as a "toxic wasteland" following Israel's extensive military assault, international humanitarian organisation Oxfam has called for an independent, field-based environmental assessment ...
item.content:encoded:
Oxfam demands independent assessment of "potential contamination" risks in Gaza strip after Israel's military action Describing Gaza as a "toxic wasteland" following Israel's extensive military assault, international humanitarian organisation Oxfam has called for an independent, field-based environmental assessment to determine the scale of contamination and its potential long-term consequences for Palestinians. ANI | Updated: 24-11-2026 10:13 IST | Created: 24-11-2026 10:13 IST

Representative Image (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

Country:

Palestine

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Describing Gaza as a "toxic wasteland" following Israel's extensive military operations, international humanitarian organisation Oxfam has called for an independent, field-based environmental assessment to determine the scale of contamination and its potential long-term consequences for Palestinians. In a new report published in collaboration with the UK-based Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS), Oxfam warned that the extensive use of explosive and incendiary weapons by the Israeli military has left Gaza's air, soil and water exposed to widespread contamination, threatening human health and survival for years and potentially decades. Titled 'Environmental War Crimes', the report examines the environmental consequences of Israel's military operations in the Palestinian territory, highlighting the widespread destruction of environmental resources and essential infrastructure. According to Oxfam, the scale and intensity of the Israeli military offensive have affected approximately 78 per cent of Gaza's land area, while its spatial analysis identified indicators of potential contamination across more than 99 per cent of the territory. The report draws on satellite-derived data, remote sensing analysis and geolocated conflict incident databases to map contamination risks across Gaza. It also uses scientific and legal literature to assess potential exposure pathways, health consequences and the legal implications of environmental destruction. Oxfam said the available evidence was already sufficient to conclude that contamination across Gaza was widespread, severe and consequential, although a comprehensive field-based investigation would be necessary to establish the precise nature and concentration of pollutants. The organisation warned that the destruction and contamination of environmental resources could expose Palestinians to serious health risks, with consequences extending well beyond the immediate period of hostilities. It also raised concerns over the implications of environmental destruction under international humanitarian law (IHL), international human rights law (IHRL) and occupation law. With international attention increasingly shifting towards the reconstruction of Gaza, Oxfam stressed that environmental recovery must not be treated as an afterthought but should be undertaken alongside rebuilding efforts. The organisation called for a full, independent and field-based Post-Conflict Environmental Assessment to establish what contaminants are present, where they are located and at what concentrations. Such an assessment, it said, would help determine the risks posed to people and the environment, identify contaminated areas and establish the measures required for remediation and long-term recovery. However, Oxfam highlighted that the absence of an independent field-based assessment was a direct consequence of Israel's continued refusal to allow independent access to Gaza. The organisation called on Israel to end its military assault and siege of Gaza and permit unrestricted access for humanitarian assistance, environmental assessments and essential equipment required for recovery. Oxfam further emphasised that reconstruction must be owned and led by Palestinians themselves and should be rights-based, reparations-oriented and rooted in accountability. It maintained that international funding for rebuilding Gaza could not replace Israel's obligation to provide reparations for harm caused by what the organisation described as unlawful acts. The environmental concerns emerge amid continuing hostilities and the destruction of essential civilian infrastructure across the Palestinian territory. Earlier, on November 18, at least six people, including a healthcare worker, patients and their companions, were killed and 27 others injured in an Israeli strike targeting the surgical department of Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Younis, southern Gaza, Al Jazeera reported, citing the Gaza Health Ministry. WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus confirmed the casualties and said the hospital's surgical department had sustained extensive damage. Other sections, including surgical theatres, the recovery unit and intensive care unit, were also reportedly affected. The WHO chief said the organisation had documented 1,056 attacks on healthcare facilities in Gaza since October 2023, resulting in 1,010 deaths and 1,725 injuries. The Israel Defence Forces (IDF), however, said the strike targeted Hamas military operatives allegedly operating from within the Nasser Hospital compound, including a senior commander of the group's Khan Younis Brigade. Meanwhile, the Israeli Prime Minister's Office has maintained that Hamas must disarm and Gaza must be demilitarised before reconstruction can begin under US President Donald Trump's 20-point plan. Israel has also highlighted its winterisation assistance and the entry of humanitarian supplies into the territory. The conflict escalated on October 7, 2023, when Hamas launched attacks on southern Israel, killing around 1,200 people and taking approximately 250 hostages, according to Israeli figures. Israel subsequently launched a large-scale military offensive in Gaza, declaring the destruction of Hamas and the return of hostages among its objectives. Oxfam warned that the environmental consequences of the conflict could persist long after the end of active hostilities, making independent assessment and environmental rehabilitation essential components of any future reconstruction programme. The organisation stressed that without identifying and addressing contamination risks, rebuilding Gaza could leave Palestinians exposed to environmental hazards for generations. (ANI)
